note:

- Question a, other: The clue 'Think about spending compared with the supply of goods' points straight at the only option that compares demand with what the economy can produce. A student can match the clue to the answer without knowing why fast growth brings inflation.

rejected.title: Growth that is too fast or too slow
card: Growth in real GDP is best when it stays near the economy's long-run trend. Growth well above or well below that trend can cause problems.
Too fast
Spending rises faster than the economy can produce. This can push up inflation, as firms raise prices when demand outruns supply.

Fast growth can also harm the environment, as more production uses more resources and creates more waste. It can put pressure on the current account, as households spend more on imports, which widens the deficit.
Too slow
Firms sell less and need fewer workers. Growth that is too slow can bring higher unemployment, as too few new jobs are created.
rejected.remember: Too fast can bring inflation, environmental harm and pressure on the current account. Too slow can bring unemployment.

a.q: Why can growth that is too fast lead to higher inflation?
opts: Demand grows faster than the economy can produce
Firms cut prices to sell more of their output
Fewer workers are hired, so wages are pushed up
Imports fall, so the price of goods rises
a.why: When spending outruns what the economy can produce, firms can raise prices and still sell their goods. The option saying imports fall reverses the effect: imports tend to rise in fast growth, as households spend more.
a.clue: Think about spending compared with the supply of goods.

b.q: Real GDP in a country grows well below its long-run trend for two years. Which outcome is most likely?
opts: Unemployment rises as too few new jobs are created
Imports surge as households spend more on foreign goods
Inflation climbs as demand outruns what is produced
Resource use and waste rise as output expands quickly
b.why: Weak growth means firms sell less and hire fewer workers, so unemployment is likely to rise. Rising imports, inflation and more waste all come from spending and output that grow too fast, not too slowly.
b.clue: Three of these come from spending that is too strong.

problems.detail: The why says 'the last option reverses the effect', meaning the imports option. Options are shown in a random order, and here the imports option is second, not last, so the explanation points students to the wrong option ('Fewer workers are hired, so wages are pushed up').
The clue 'Slow growth means firms need fewer workers' all but states the right option. Only one option is about workers or jobs, so students can match the clue without understanding the idea.

'harm' on its own is vague; the card means environmental harm. 'import pressure' also loosely stands in for pressure on the current account. Saying 'environmental harm' and 'pressure on the current account' would match the card.

a.q: A country's real GDP grows well above its long-run trend for several years. Which is the most likely effect on prices?
opts: Inflation rises as firms raise prices when demand is strong
Inflation falls as firms cut prices to attract more buyers
Inflation falls as imports replace locally made goods
Inflation rises as fewer workers are hired by firms
a.why: Fast growth means spending is strong, so firms can raise prices and still sell their goods. The option about fewer workers being hired describes weak growth, not fast growth, and it does not explain rising prices.
a.clue: Ask what firms can do with prices when buyers are plentiful.

b.q: Real GDP in a country grows well below its long-run trend for two years. Which outcome is most likely?
opts: Unemployment rises as firms sell less and hire fewer workers
Unemployment falls as firms cut costs and hire more workers
The current account deficit widens as imports rise sharply
Inflation rises as firms put up prices to protect profits
b.why: Weak growth means firms sell less and need fewer workers, so unemployment is likely to rise. A wider deficit and rising inflation come from spending that grows too fast, and falling unemployment reverses the effect.
b.clue: Think about what happens to hiring when firms sell less.

a.best: Inflation rises as firms raise prices when demand is strong
